analysis.one_liner: Creates federally funded state plans guaranteeing universal, affordable health insurance coverage to all residents.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in two House committees from May 2005 until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given states federal matching funds to cover uninsured residents, starting with families earning up to 300% of the poverty line, with strict caps on premiums and out-of-pocket costs. By 2010, every state would have had to guarantee coverage to all residents, and most employers would have had to pay at least 80% of their employees' health insurance premiums. It also would have barred preexisting-condition exclusions, required mental health parity in Medicare, and folded in patient-protection and medical-error reduction measures. It was referred to two House committees and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 45 million uninsured Americans the bill cited, especially low- and moderate-income families who would receive heavily subsidized coverage with no preexisting-condition exclusions, capped premiums and cost-sharing, and a guaranteed benefits package. Low-wage workers would benefit from the employer contribution mandate, and home care workers from new employer-of-record and job-protection standards.

how_it_helps.text: States would receive open-ended federal matching funds to cover residents up to 300% of the poverty line, with states allowed to extend coverage to everyone, and would have to reach 100% coverage of eligible residents within four years of plan approval [S3].

Premiums and cost-sharing would be tightly capped: families below 150% of poverty would pay no premium and at most 0.5% of income in cost-sharing, and no preexisting-condition exclusions would be allowed [S3].

Most employers would have to enroll workers in state purchasing pools and pay at least 80% of premiums, capped at 10% of an employee's wages, enforceable by employees in court with attorney's fees [S3].

Medicare beneficiaries would receive full mental health and substance abuse treatment parity beginning in 2006, and the bill would incorporate patient-protection and whistleblower measures from prior Senate-passed bills [S2][S3].
States would have to limit plans' administrative costs and profits to at most 10% of premium income, and states could choose a single-payer system exempt from the employer mandate [S3].

Home care workers would gain an employer of record for payroll, unemployment insurance, and workers' compensation, plus advance notice of closures and a right of first refusal for displaced positions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, which would owe at least 80% of employees' premium costs (up to 10% of wages); health insurers and health plans, which would face a 90% medical-loss requirement, competitive bidding, and the possibility of state single-payer systems; and federal taxpayers, since the bill authorized 'such sums as may be necessary' with only a non-binding sense of Congress that costs be offset by surpluses, health savings, or reduced tax benefits for top-bracket individuals and large corporations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, health plans, and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The federal appropriation was open-ended ('such sums as may be necessary'), and the proposed offsets — budget surpluses, speculative health savings, and tax-benefit reductions — were only a non-binding sense of Congress, so the bill had no credible financing mechanism attached [S3].
The employer mandate requiring 80% premium contributions, capped at 10% of wages, would have been a significant new labor cost for covered employers, particularly smaller firms [S3].

Requiring every state to reach universal coverage by a fixed date, with residents able to sue their state in federal court for failing to submit a plan, would have forced difficult state budget and design decisions on a short timeline [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — universal, affordable coverage with no preexisting-condition exclusions and strict cost-sharing caps — would be large and directly felt by the 45 million uninsured the bill identified. The honest cost is money: an open-ended federal entitlement with no binding pay-for, plus real new costs for employers and constraints on health plans. The design was detailed but ambitious, and its two-phase state-by-state structure carried real implementation and financing risk. Whether the trade was worth it is a policy judgment; what is certain from the record is that no committee ever weighed it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2005, referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees and then to their health subcommittees, and nothing further ever happened to it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tammy Baldwin and 13 original cosponsors introduced the bill on May 5, 2005, to guarantee all Americans quality, affordable, comprehensive health insurance [S3].

It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, then to the health subcommittees of both, and the action record shows no hearings, markups, or floor action thereafter [S5].
Nineteen Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on [S4].
The bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, without either committee ever reporting it [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have owed the 80% premium mandate and health plans that avoided the 90% medical-loss floor and competitive bidding were spared; the 45 million uninsured the bill described gained nothing. The bill's death also preserved the status quo in which coverage depends on employment and income.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and health plans that would have faced mandates

for.name: Rep. Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor in September 2005.

for.name: 19 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 19 were Democrats, including original cosponsors such as Reps. Schakowsky, Conyers, Rangel, Stark, and Obey.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in May 2005 and sent it to its Health Subcommittee; never held a markup or reported the bill.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in May 2005 and sent it to its Health Subcommittee; never acted on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 19 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill died in committees controlled by the Republican majority without any vote ever being taken.

industries.note: The bill routes new publicly funded coverage through state-approved 'qualified plans,' giving insurers a large subsidized customer base — but it caps administration and profit at 10% of premium income, forces annual competitive bidding, lets states choose a single-payer system, and lifts ERISA preemption for plan-based coverage, all of which threaten the industry's current position.

Employers with fewer than 500 employees would have to enroll every worker in a state purchasing pool and pay at least 80% of premiums (capped at 10% of wages), with employee lawsuits and attorney's fees for noncompliance. Their cost is the funding source for worker coverage.

industries.industry: Home care agencies and staffing entities
industries.note: Plans would have to create or contract with an employer of record covering payroll, unemployment insurance, and workers' compensation for home care workers, plus advance notice of service changes and right-of-first-refusal hiring for displaced workers — real costs to entities that currently avoid those obligations.

industries.industry: Wealthiest households and large corporations in the top tax brackets
industries.note: The bill's sense of Congress says implementation costs should be offset by reducing 'unnecessary Federal tax benefits' available only to top-bracket individuals and large corporations, though the provision is non-binding.
